props.title: The House Is Black

sections.content: The House Is Black stands as one of cinema's most powerful explorations of human dignity and social isolation. Iranian poet Forough Farrokhzad's only film - a 22-minute documentary shot in a leper colony - revolutionized Iranian cinema and influenced directors like Abbas Kiarostami and Mohsen Makhmalbaf. The film's unflinching yet deeply poetic approach to documenting marginalized people created a template for humanitarian cinema, later echoed in works like Sans Soleil (1983) and Homeless (1989).

sections.content: The film's revolutionary fusion of poetry and documentary technique transformed how filmmakers approach social issues. Farrokhzad's lyrical voiceover, reading both religious texts and her own poetry over stark black-and-white footage, created a new language for documentary filmmaking. This approach influenced works like Night and Fog (1956) and later The Act of Killing (2012), where artistic expression meets documentary reality.

The film's treatment of its subjects - showing their humanity while never flinching from their medical condition - set new standards for ethical documentary filmmaking. Unlike exploitation documentaries of the era, Farrokhzad spent 12 days living in the colony, developing relationships with its inhabitants. This approach influenced later works like In the Year of the Pig (1968) and Hospital (1970). SUBHEAD: Impact on Global Documentary Movement

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond Iran, impacting global documentary practices. Its poetic-realist approach can be seen in works like Chris Marker's essays and Agnès Varda's social documentaries. The film's ability to find beauty in suffering while maintaining dignity influenced contemporary filmmakers like Wang Bing and Pedro Costa, seen in films like Three Sisters (2012) and In Vanda's Room (2000).
